series.title: What Does It Take To Have A Successful Marriage?
series.description: In Genesis 2:24, God declares that a man shall leave his father and mother, hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. Yet today, we witness countless divorces, separations, and marriages sustained by unhealthy forbearance. Why? What does it truly take to build a successful marriage? Could the answer lie in a foundation we often overlook - honesty?

episodes.title: What Does It Take To Have A Successful Marriage?

sections.heading: God's Design for Companionship
message: From the beginning, the Bible tells us that it is not good for man to be alone.

Throughout creation, after God created something, He declared it good. In Genesis 1:31, God looked at everything He had made and declared it very good. Yet Genesis 2:18 reveals something significant: God said it was not good for the man to be alone.

This was not a contradiction. Genesis 1 gives us the overview of creation, while Genesis 2 zooms in on the creation of man. There God points out the one thing still lacking: a companion. Human beings were created for relationship and community, not isolation.

sections.heading: A Suitable Helper, Not a Subordinate
message: God declared that He would make a suitable helper for Adam.

The Hebrew expression ezer kenegdo, often translated as “suitable helper,” carries a deeper meaning than the English word “helper” might suggest. It describes someone corresponding to him, a counterpart, an ally, someone suited to stand alongside him rather than someone of lesser worth. The word ezer is also used elsewhere in Scripture of God Himself as our help, which shows it does not describe someone inferior.

The foundation of marriage in Genesis recognizes the spouse as a partner of equal human worth and value. Marriage was not designed around one person’s humanity being more important than the other’s. It was established as a relationship of companionship and shared life.

The Hebrew expression *ezer kenegdo*, often translated as “*suitable helper*,” carries a deeper meaning than the English word “*helper*” might suggest. It describes someone corresponding to him, a counterpart, an ally, someone suited to stand alongside him rather than someone of lesser worth. The foundation of marriage in Genesis recognizes the spouse as a partner of equal human worth and value. Marriage was not designed around one person’s humanity being more important than the other’s. It was established as a relationship of companionship and shared life.

sections.heading: Leaving and Becoming One
message: The Bible tells us that a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.

Jesus Himself quotes this passage in Matthew 19, pointing His listeners back to God’s original design. Marriage is not a human invention or a social arrangement. It is something God established, and that is why how we enter it and how we treat it matters.
Here, we see the establishment of boundaries.

Marriage creates a new family relationship in which the spouse becomes the primary partner, taking priority over parents, siblings, and other outside relationships. This does not mean abandoning family or cutting off every other relationship. It means establishing an independent household where the couple makes decisions together without allowing outside relationships to govern their marriage.
The couple must recognize that their marriage is now a shared responsibility.

sections.heading: Are Communication, Commitment, and Intimacy Enough?
message: When people discuss successful marriages, they often mention commitment, communication, respect, emotional intelligence, and intimacy.
These are all important. But are they enough?

We know people who communicate exceptionally well. We know people who are respectful, emotionally intelligent, self-aware, and capable of understanding others. Yet these qualities do not automatically produce a successful marriage.

Communication, for example, does not necessarily mean honesty. Two people can communicate regularly while withholding the truth. Someone can express feelings clearly while concealing intentions. A person can be respectful and still avoid acknowledging what they truly want. These qualities help sustain a relationship, but they raise a deeper question: What must exist for these qualities to operate genuinely?

sections.heading: Honesty Before Commitment
message: One of the foundational pillars of a successful marriage is honesty. Not simply honesty with the person we are marrying, but honesty with ourselves.

Honesty allows two people to know from the beginning what they are entering, how they intend to approach it, what they can offer, and what they cannot accept. It allows us to be ourselves without permitting emotions, temporary feelings, or particular moments to pressure us into telling someone what they want to hear.

Sometimes, because we love someone or fear losing them, we make promises that do not reflect who we truly are. We agree to things we know we cannot comfortably accept. We present ourselves as people we hope to become rather than acknowledging who we actually are. The problem is that marriage is not built merely upon the emotions experienced when promises are made. It must also survive the realities that follow.
Scripture calls us to put away falsehood and speak truth to one another. Honesty is not just a good habit in marriage. It is part of how God calls His people to live.

In Luke 14:28, Jesus uses the illustration of someone considering building a tower who first calculates the cost. Although the passage concerns discipleship, the principle of understanding the cost of a commitment is worth considering in marriage. Honesty allows both individuals to make a lifelong decision based on reality rather than expectations.

sections.heading: When Forbearance Becomes a Way of Life
message: Forbearance is an important part of marriage. No two people are identical, and differences, weaknesses, and imperfections require patience, grace, and understanding. Scripture is clear that we are to bear with one another and forgive as Christ forgave us.

But there is a difference between forbearance and silence. Healthy forbearance is the willing choice to extend grace to someone we know and have honestly chosen. It is offered freely, and it leaves room for truth to be spoken in love.

Unhealthy forbearance looks different. It develops when we hide who we are or what we cannot accept, and then endure quietly to keep the peace. Colossians 3:13 does not tell us to bury the truth. It tells us to bear with one another and forgive, which assumes there is something real to be acknowledged and forgiven.

Let me be clear: this is not an invitation to leave a marriage because it is hard or because a spouse is imperfect. Every marriage requires patience and sacrifice. The question is not “Is this difficult?” but “Have we been honest with each other, and are we working through this together?” Where there is abuse or serious harm, a spouse should seek safety and wise counsel from a pastor or counselor rather than simply endure.

A couple can remain married for decades while one or both spouses spend those years enduring a reality they never honestly acknowledged. This raises an important question: Is remaining married the same as having a successful marriage? Longevity alone does not establish success.

sections.heading: Honesty With Yourself
message: Being honest with another person begins with the willingness to examine ourselves. We must be willing to acknowledge our limitations, our intentions, our expectations, and our contributions to the difficulties within our relationships. Sometimes we are quick to identify what our spouse is doing wrong while refusing to examine our own behavior.

In Genesis 3:12, when God confronted Adam, Adam pointed toward the woman who had given him the fruit. His statement contained a fact, but it also shifted attention away from his own responsibility. The greatest obstacle to honesty is not an outright lie. It is using part of the truth to avoid acknowledging our own responsibility. A person cannot genuinely take responsibility for something they refuse to recognize.
Honesty with ourselves makes accountability possible.

sections.heading: Marriage Requires Two Willing People
message: There are many things an individual can accomplish alone. We can develop communication skills, improve emotional intelligence, become more patient, seek counseling, and work on our personal weaknesses. However, marriage is not an individual achievement. It requires two people. One person cannot create mutual trust alone. One person cannot establish mutual commitment alone. One person cannot force another to be honest, faithful, or willing to grow.

There may be seasons when one spouse carries more responsibility because of illness, hardship, or other circumstances. Marriage does not require both individuals to contribute equally in every moment. However, a genuine partnership requires both individuals to recognize and accept their shared responsibility.

Scripture reminds us that two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. But two must be willing to walk together. The purpose of marriage is not for one person to continually hold together what two people have committed to build.

sections.heading: Is Honesty Enough?
message: Honesty is foundational, but honesty alone does not guarantee a successful marriage. Two people may be honest about their differences and still be unable to build a healthy relationship together.

Honesty reveals the truth. Love determines how we respond to it. Scripture puts it this way: we are to speak “the truth in love.” Truth without love wounds, and love without truth deceives. Both must work together.

Commitment helps us remain engaged in the work of building and sustaining the relationship. Communication, respect, intimacy, patience, and forgiveness remain essential, but without honesty, these qualities can become performances rather than a genuine expression of partnership.

So the question is not only “Do we love each other?” It is “Do we truly know each other, and did we choose each other honestly?” If we can answer yes, the work of building a marriage can begin on solid ground.

sections.heading: Where Do We Go From Here?
message: If you are not yet married, ask the hard questions now. What do you expect? What can you offer? What can you not accept? Say it plainly, even when it is uncomfortable, because a marriage built on pretending is built on sand.

If you are already married, it is not too late. Honest marriage begins with honest self-examination. Ask God to search your heart, and be willing to name your own part in the difficulties, not only your spouse’s.

Then speak truth in love. Choose a calm moment rather than the middle of an argument. Say what you actually think and feel, and listen without defending yourself. Honesty only survives where it is safe, so both spouses must make it safe for the other to be truthful.
You do not have to do this alone. Seek wise counsel from a pastor, a mature couple, or a counselor. Honest marriage is built one truthful conversation at a time, and no one is too far along to begin.

sections.heading: Conclusion
message: Finally, a successful marriage is not simply the result of two people loving each other, communicating regularly, or remaining together for many years. It begins with two individuals who are willing to be truthful about who they are, what they believe, what they expect, what they can offer, and what they cannot accept.

Honesty does not eliminate differences, disagreements, or the need for sacrifice. It allows two people to face those realities without pretending. Marriage will require patience. It will require forgiveness, compromise, commitment, and sometimes significant sacrifice.
But there is a difference between willingly making sacrifices for someone we have honestly chosen and spending a lifetime enduring a situation we entered by denying who we truly were.

Honesty is also not a weapon. We are not telling the truth to win arguments or to demand our own way. We are telling the truth in love, so that two people can know each other fully and stay committed anyway.

The foundation of a successful marriage is not pretending to be everything another person wants. It is allowing two people to know and choose each other truthfully, then continuing to build their life together with love, accountability, and mutual commitment.
Questions for Reflection (all flush left):

1. Am I honest with myself about what I expect from marriage and what I am willing to give?
2. Have I ever made a promise simply because I feared disappointing or losing someone?
3. Do I accept my spouse for who they are, or am I depending on who I hope they will become? (People grow, but love should not depend on a version of them that doesn’t exist yet.)
4. Am I practicing patience out of love, or silently enduring something I have never honestly addressed?
5. When did we last have an honest conversation about something difficult, and what kept us from having it sooner?
6. If you are not yet married: Have I told this person plainly what I expect and what I cannot accept?

episodes.prayer:
Heavenly Father,

Thank You for creating us for companionship and for teaching us the importance of love, faithfulness, and unity.

Give us the courage to be honest with ourselves and with those we love. Help us recognize our limitations, acknowledge our mistakes, and speak the truth with humility and compassion.

Teach us not to make promises merely to satisfy temporary emotions, but to approach our commitments with wisdom and understanding.

Where there are differences, give us patience. Where there are misunderstandings, give us clarity. Where there are failures, give us humility and the willingness to change.

Help us build marriages grounded in truth, strengthened by love, and sustained through mutual faithfulness.

In Jesus’ name, Amen.

series.title: Understanding Anger Through Scripture
series.description: Is anger a sin? Scripture shows God, Jesus, and even ordinary people experiencing anger, yet it also warns how quickly anger can lead us into sin. What is the difference between righteous and unrighteous anger, and how can wisdom govern what we do with it?

episodes.title: Understanding Anger Through Scripture

sections.heading: What Is Anger?
message: Anger is a basic human emotion characterized by a strong feeling of displeasure in response to perceived threats, injustice, unfair treatment, hurt, frustration, or violations of personal and social boundaries.

Anger can function as a defense or survival mechanism. When people experience danger, mistreatment, or injustice, anger may motivate them to protect themselves, establish boundaries, confront wrongdoing, or seek change.
Anger is neither inherently good nor bad. It is a powerful emotion, and its power works in both directions.
On one hand, anger can motivate positive change, encourage people to stand against injustice, protect others, and establish healthy boundaries.
On the other hand, anger can damage relationships, impair judgment, lead to aggression or violence, and negatively affect physical and emotional health when it becomes chronic.
This raises an important question: Is anger a sin?

sections.heading: Is Anger a Sin?
message: From a biblical perspective, anger itself cannot be considered inherently sinful, because Scripture repeatedly describes God as expressing anger. God is holy, righteous, and without sin, so His anger cannot originate from sinful motives. It is an expression of His holiness and justice, directed toward wickedness, oppression, rebellion, and wrongdoing.

Yet the Bible also describes God as slow to anger. Exodus 34:6-7 reveals Him as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and it adds that He will by no means clear the guilty. His slowness to anger is an expression of His mercy and patience, giving people opportunities to repent and return to Him. It does not mean He tolerates evil indefinitely or abandons justice.

The clearest evidence for human anger comes from Jesus. Scripture says He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. It also records Him looking around at religious leaders "with anger" (Mark 3:5). If Jesus, who never sinned, experienced anger, then anger itself cannot be sin.
However, our anger must be examined more carefully than God's, because human nature has been affected by sin. What is sinless in Him can easily become sinful in us.

sections.heading: Two Expressions of Anger
message: From our biblical examination, anger can be distinguished into two broad categories: righteous anger and unrighteous anger.

Righteous anger is a morally justified response to wrongdoing, motivated by truth, justice, and love, and governed by wisdom and self-control. It may arise when we witness injustice, oppression, mistreatment, or the misuse of God's name.

However, having a righteous cause does not automatically make our response righteous. Defending what is right does not necessarily mean we are doing what is right. For anger to remain righteous, we must examine not only the wrongdoing that provoked it but also our motivations, intentions, and responses.

Unrighteous anger arises from or develops into sinful motives and attitudes such as pride, jealousy, hatred, bitterness, selfishness, and revenge. It can cause people to act impulsively, disregard truth, harm others, or pursue personal retaliation rather than justice.

Unrighteous anger does not always result in outward violence. It may also be expressed internally through cultivated hatred, resentment, or malicious intentions. In Matthew 5:21-22, Jesus teaches that anger goes beyond the physical act of murder and addresses the moral condition of the heart. Anger can become sinful both through our internal attitudes and through our outward actions.

sections.heading: Cain: When Anger Opens the Door to Sin
message: Cain became angry when God regarded Abel's offering but did not regard his own.
Before Cain killed Abel, God confronted him about his anger and warned him that sin was crouching at the door. God told Cain that he must rule over it.

This passage reveals an important lesson: Cain had an opportunity to examine his anger and respond differently. Instead, his resentment developed into an act of violence against his brother. His murder of Abel was not merely an isolated act. It followed a failure to respond rightly to his anger and to God's warning.
Cain's story demonstrates how anger, when influenced by sinful desires and left unchecked, can lead to devastating consequences.
The lesson: We must recognize anger before it begins governing our judgment and behavior.

sections.heading: Jesus: Righteous Anger Against Wrongdoing
message: Jesus provides examples of righteous opposition to wrongdoing.

In John 2, Jesus entered the temple and found merchants and money changers conducting business there. He drove them out and confronted the misuse of His Father's house. His actions demonstrated zeal for God's house rather than personal revenge.

In Mark 3, Jesus became angry at the hardness of heart of religious leaders who opposed healing on the Sabbath. Scripture says He was also grieved by their hardness of heart. His anger was connected to their lack of compassion.

These examples show that righteous anger is not necessarily passive or silent. Sometimes confronting wrongdoing requires firm action. However, righteous anger must remain consistent with righteousness: it is motivated by truth, mixed with compassion, and free from personal revenge.
The lesson: Strong opposition to evil can be righteous when motivated by truth and governed by wisdom.

sections.heading: Jonah: When Personal Judgment Opposes God's Mercy
message: God sent Jonah to Nineveh to warn the people about their wickedness. Nineveh had genuinely committed evil, and God's warning was justified.
However, when the people repented and God showed mercy, Jonah became angry. He believed Nineveh deserved punishment, but he was unwilling to accept God's decision to show mercy.

Jonah's prayer in Jonah 4:2 is revealing. He admits that he knew God is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger, the same description we saw in Exodus 34. Jonah agreed with that truth about God until it applied to people he thought deserved judgment.

His anger was not simply a response to injustice. It reflected his personal dissatisfaction with God's compassion toward the people. This reveals the difference between recognizing wrongdoing and assuming the authority to determine how others must be judged.
The lesson: Our anger becomes unrighteous when personal desires, resentment, or pride take precedence over God's righteousness and mercy.

sections.heading: Moses: When Frustration Overrides Wisdom
message: Moses had spent years leading the Israelites through the wilderness, repeatedly dealing with their complaints and dissatisfaction.

When the people complained about the lack of water, God instructed Moses to speak to the rock. Instead, Moses spoke harshly to the people and struck the rock twice. Psalm 106 explains that the people provoked Moses and that he spoke rashly.

Moses allowed the pressure and frustration caused by the people to influence his judgment. Although their complaints were real, their behavior did not justify his disobedience. God disciplined Moses because he failed to trust Him and honor Him as holy before the Israelites.
This account demonstrates that even a legitimate reason for frustration does not justify acting contrary to God's instruction.
The lesson: When frustration governs our judgment instead of wisdom, even a legitimate grievance can lead to sinful behavior.

sections.heading: Paul's Teaching: Be Angry, but Do Not Sin
message: Paul instructs believers to be angry without sinning, and he warns against letting the sun go down on our anger. He adds that anger left alone gives the devil an opportunity.

This passage makes an important distinction between experiencing anger and allowing anger to lead us into sin. Anger does not automatically require sinful behavior. We have a responsibility to govern how we respond. The warning about the sun going down is practical: anger that we carry overnight, unaddressed, tends to harden into something worse.

Paul also warns against allowing anger to develop into bitterness, hostility, and malice. Ephesians 4:31 instructs believers to put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander, and malice. The emphasis is not simply on controlling outward behavior but also on preventing anger from becoming a destructive disposition within the heart.
In Romans 12:19, Paul addresses the desire for revenge directly: do not take vengeance, but leave room for God's wrath. When we are wronged, justice is not ours to administer on our own terms.
The lesson: We may experience anger, but we must not allow it to control our thoughts, intentions, or actions.

sections.heading: James: Understanding the Desires Behind Anger
message: James teaches that believers should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger. He explains that the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.

This can seem to conflict with righteous anger, but James is describing how human anger usually behaves. Left to itself, our anger rarely produces what God desires. That is why James urges us to be slow to anger, and it supports the care Scripture asks us to take.

James also connects quarrels and conflicts to desires struggling within people. This reveals that anger does not always arise from genuine injustice. Sometimes anger develops because our expectations are not met, our pride is wounded, our desires are frustrated, or we feel threatened.
Therefore, before responding to anger, we must examine its source. Are we angry because something is genuinely wrong, or because something did not happen the way we wanted?
The lesson: Understanding why we are angry is essential to determining whether our response will be righteous.

sections.heading: Wisdom: The Key to Responding Righteously
message: Wisdom plays a central role in how we handle anger. Anger is an emotional response, but wisdom helps us determine whether and how we should act.

Proverbs 29:11 teaches that a fool gives full expression to his anger, while a wise person exercises restraint. Proverbs 19:11 connects good sense with being slow to anger. Proverbs 16:32 goes further: one who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and one who rules his spirit is better than one who takes a city.

Wisdom also shapes how we speak. Proverbs 15:1 says that a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. These passages demonstrate that wisdom does not necessarily prevent anger from arising. Instead, wisdom governs our response.
A person may have every reason to be angry but still make an unwise decision. Wisdom allows us to evaluate the situation, consider the consequences, and determine the appropriate response.

Self-control is equally important. Wisdom helps us recognize what is right, while self-control helps us carry it out. Without wisdom, anger can distort judgment. Without self-control, even a person who knows what is right may act impulsively.
Anger may alert us that something is wrong, but wisdom must determine what we do about it.

sections.heading: God's Patience: An Example for Human Anger
message: God's character provides an important example of how anger can coexist with patience and mercy. Throughout Scripture, God demonstrates that being slow to anger is not a sign of weakness. It is an expression of His mercy and patience.

Ezekiel 33:11 reveals God's desire that the wicked turn from their ways and live. 2 Peter 3:9 connects God's patience with His desire for repentance. God does not abandon justice, but His patience allows opportunities for people to turn from wrongdoing.
Human beings are not God and do not possess His perfect judgment. Nevertheless, Scripture calls us to reflect His character in how we respond to others.
Being slow to anger does not mean ignoring injustice or refusing to confront wrongdoing. It means refusing to allow anger to become the controlling force behind our decisions.
The lesson: Patience creates room for wisdom to guide our response rather than allowing frustration to dictate our actions.

sections.heading: Examining Our Anger
message: When God asked Jonah, "Do you do well to be angry?", He was inviting him to examine his own heart. Before responding to anger, we should do the same by considering four questions.
The cause: Why am I angry? Is there genuine wrongdoing, or am I reacting to personal frustration, wounded pride, or disappointed expectations?
The heart: What is motivating my anger? Am I seeking justice and truth, or am I motivated by resentment, hatred, jealousy, or revenge?
The response: Am I allowing wisdom and self-control to govern my behavior, or am I reacting impulsively?
The purpose: What am I trying to accomplish? Am I seeking correction, protection, and justice, or simply trying to make someone suffer?
These questions help us distinguish between anger that can lead to righteous action and anger that may lead us into sin.

sections.heading: What Do We Do With Our Anger?
message: Knowing the difference between righteous and unrighteous anger is only the beginning. We also need to know what to do when anger rises.
First, pause. Wisdom needs time, and anger rarely gives it any. Stepping back, breathing, and refusing to answer in the heat of the moment gives wisdom room to speak.
Second, bring it to God. The psalmist invites us to be angry and not sin, to reflect quietly, and to pour out our hearts before Him. God is not surprised by our anger, and He can handle it honestly.
Third, examine it using the four questions: the cause, the heart, the response, and the purpose.
Fourth, if the anger is rooted in genuine wrongdoing, respond with truth and gentleness. Address the problem, not the person's worth, and seek correction and resolution rather than revenge.
Fifth, forgive. Do not let the sun go down on your anger. Forgiveness does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen or removing every consequence. It means refusing to let bitterness take root.
Finally, do not carry it alone. Seek wise counsel from a pastor, a mature believer, or a counselor.

If you have been seriously wronged or harmed, your anger is not automatically sinful, and you do not have to suppress it or pretend nothing happened. Where there is abuse or danger, seek safety and wise help first. Anger can be a signal that something is wrong. The goal is not to silence that signal, but to make sure it leads somewhere wise.

sections.heading: Conclusion
message: Anger is part of the human emotional experience. It can arise from injustice, threats, disappointment, fear, frustration, or personal hurt.
The Bible does not teach that every experience of anger is sinful. God expresses righteous anger toward evil. Jesus confronted wrongdoing. Paul acknowledged anger while warning believers not to sin.

However, Scripture also demonstrates the destructive consequences of anger when it is governed by pride, resentment, selfish desires, or uncontrolled frustration. Cain allowed resentment to lead him into murder. Jonah allowed personal judgment to oppose God's mercy. Moses allowed frustration to influence his obedience. Jesus, by contrast, demonstrated righteous opposition to wrongdoing, and Paul and James instructed believers to govern anger through righteous conduct, patience, and restraint.

The central lesson is that anger must never become the authority that determines our actions. Wisdom must guide our judgment, self-control must govern our behavior, and righteousness must shape our motives.
We cannot always prevent anger from arising, but we can learn to respond to it wisely.
Anger is an emotion, not a command. We may feel it, but we do not have to obey it.

episodes.prayer:
Heavenly Father,

Thank You for being patient with us, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.

When anger rises in us, help us pause before we speak or act. Search our hearts and show us the true source of our anger, whether it is injustice, wounded pride, disappointed expectations, or unforgiveness.

Give us wisdom to know what is right and self-control to do it. Keep us from revenge, bitterness, and harsh words. Where we have been wronged, give us courage to seek truth and justice without hatred.

Teach us to forgive as You have forgiven us, and do not let us carry our anger into the night.

For those who are carrying deep hurt, surround them with wise and caring people, and bring healing.

In Jesus' name, Amen.
